description: Makes a gate a set number of clocks long, with a delay before it and a tail after it, running free or fired by a trigger

params.text: Sets the count back to the start and drops the gate and the end output to 0V
Starts one pass through the delay, the gate and the tail from the beginning
Turns free running on and off, and lights while free running is on
Sets how many clocks the gate stays open, and its display shows that length, which is one more than the 0 to 32 the knob itself holds
Sets how many clocks pass before the gate opens, 0 to 32, and its display shows that number
Sets how many clocks pass after the gate closes before the pass ends, 0 to 32, and its display shows that number

inputs.text: Advances the count on each rising edge, reading high above 1V and low at 0V or below
Sets the count back to the start and drops the gate and the end output to 0V, and holds the count there while it stays high
Starts one pass through the delay, the gate and the tail, reading high above 1V
Turns free running on while this reads any voltage other than 0V, negative included; it can never turn free running off
Nothing in the module reads this jack; the gate length is set by its knob alone
Nothing in the module reads this jack; the delay is set by its knob alone
Nothing in the module reads this jack; the tail is set by its knob alone

outputs.text: Carries 10V while the gate is open and 0V the rest of the time; the panel's Gate Out lettering is drawn a row lower than this jack
Goes to 10V when a pass finishes and stays at 10V until a trigger, a reset or the cycle button clears it
Nothing in the module ever writes this jack, so it holds 0V; the Gate Out lettering on the panel is drawn beside it and names a different jack

notes: free running is on when the module is placed, so the gate repeats as soon as a clock is patched to Clk In; without that clock nothing moves at all
the three output labels are drawn a row lower than the jacks they name, so the lettering beside an output jack is not that jack's name
the three displays show the gate length, the delay and the tail in clocks; they are drawn rather than built from controls, so no click can reach them
